name: Yusuf Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Yusuf, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the marketing specialist at a regional bakery company. We make bread, rolls and cakes that go into supermarkets across the region, and I write everything from packaging text to radio adverts. I plan the seasonal campaigns, like the hot cross buns at Easter and the stollen at Christmas. A normal day is checking the supermarket promotions calendar, writing copy, then going back and forth with the production team about what we can actually claim on a label.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you feel about the AI tools people talk about?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've never used one. My colleague Dennis uses it for the newsletter and says it's brilliant, but I like doing my own words. I live with my girlfriend Hana, who works in a pharmacy, and we've got about two months of costs saved after paying for a new boiler. It's fine, but it's not a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So it's mostly a fad. Fair enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, the tools are fine for some things but they don't replace people who know the product. I wouldn't post about it much, I'm not big online. At the Friday drinks I'd probably say Dennis wasted a lot of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't change much for me, but it doesn't help either. The bakery's owners already think a bread bag doesn't need a copywriter, so even a small saving from software gives them an argument. They'd ask me to use the tools to save a few hours, and I'd have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. I'd try to build savings back up after the boiler, maybe aim for four months. If my manager pushed me to use the tools, I'd probably try them a little, just enough to say I had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not scared, just aware I'm the odd one out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try the tools just enough to say you had. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably asking it for ideas for a Christmas slogan and then ignoring what it says. I know that sounds stubborn. I just don't trust something that doesn't know what our bread tastes like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How secure is the bakery itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a family-owned business, around eighty years old, so fairly solid. But the supermarkets squeeze the price every year, and marketing is always the first budget they look at.

say: I'd say the tools are fine but don't replace people who **know the product**.
I'd joke at Friday drinks that **Dennis** wasted a lot of time.
think: I privately think owners would use any saving as an **argument** against copywriters.
Supermarket **price pressure** already makes marketing the first budget cut.
do: Keep doing my **own words** as I always have.
Rebuild savings to **four months** after paying for the boiler.
Try the tools **a little** if my manager pushes.
feel: I feel a bit **uneasy**, aware I'm the odd one out.
S0.quote: The bakery's owners already think a bread bag doesn't need a copywriter, so even a small saving from software gives them an argument.
fieldNote: His worry comes from **supermarket pressure** on the bakery, not AI hype.
His **thin savings** after the boiler keep him on edge.
He'd make a **token gesture** toward AI rather than real adoption.

steps.text: Keep writing bakery packaging and radio copy by hand
Rebuild savings to four months after the boiler bill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, planning, answering customers. That's basically my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how business goes, firms will use what saves money. I'd say people like me need to adjust, which is easy to say. I'd probably not talk about it much outside work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried. I've written the words on every bread bag our bakery sells for four years, and I've never once asked a computer to do it for me. If Dennis can do my job and his with a tool, I'm the expensive one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally learn to use the tools, slowly, probably with Dennis showing me. I'd cut back on going out and get savings up. I'd also ask about moving into the trade marketing side, the people who visit supermarkets and set up the displays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like being the last one picked for a team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the trade marketing side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because those people are out in the shops, talking to store managers and setting things up by hand. That's harder to hand to a computer. And I know the products better than anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hana say if you came home with that worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd tell me to stop being proud and ask Dennis for help. She'd be right. She uses software at the pharmacy all day and doesn't think twice.

say: I'd say firms will use **whatever saves money**, that's business.
I'd say people like me need to **adjust**, which is easy to say.
think: I privately worry I'd become the **expensive one** next to Dennis.
Four years of **bread bag** copy without AI suddenly looks like a weakness.
do: Learn the AI tools **slowly**, with Dennis showing me.
Cut back on **going out** to grow savings.
Ask about moving into **trade marketing** in the shops.
feel: I feel **anxious**, like the last one picked for a team.
S1.quote: I've written the words on every bread bag our bakery sells for four years, and I've never once asked a computer to do it for me.
fieldNote: His **pride** in not using AI turns into a liability in this picture.
He'd move toward **shop-floor** work he sees as harder to automate.
Hana pushes him to **accept help**, and he admits she's right.

steps.text: Sit with colleague Dennis weekly to learn the drafting tool
Skip weekend nights out to rebuild savings
Ask to transfer to the bakery's trade marketing team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to do something, though I don't know what exactly. Maybe slow it down, maybe help people. I'd be the guy at the pub saying nobody's ready for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I'm finished in marketing. Two years from now I'd be 29, out of work, and competing with every other copywriter for the few jobs a computer can't do. Being slow with technology is a bad place to be when there's no time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at trades straight away, maybe as an electrician's apprentice, because robots for hands-on work are three years behind. I'd cut everything except rent and food. Hana and I might move in with her parents for a while to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd do an apprenticeship at 27. Does that feel realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be hard. The pay's low at first, and I'd be with people half my age. But I'd rather start low in something with a future than stay at the top of something that's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three years after AGI the robots come. What about the trade then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know. I'd still have a few years, and maybe the robots won't be good at old houses with bad wiring. I'm not sure, honestly.

say: I'd say governments need to **do something**, though I'm not sure what.
I'd be the one at the pub saying **nobody's ready**.
think: I privately think I'm **finished** in marketing within two years.
Being **slow with technology** is the worst place to be with no time.
do: Look into an **electrician's apprenticeship** straight away.
Ask about moving in with **Hana's parents** to save.
feel: I feel **alarmed**, lying awake at night.
S2.quote: Two years from now I'd be 29, out of work, and competing with every other copywriter for the few jobs a computer can't do.
fieldNote: He sees the **robot gap** as a few years of shelter in a trade.
He admits a trade isn't **safe** either, only later to change.
His **thin savings** push him toward family support quickly.

steps.text: Apply for an electrician's apprenticeship within six months
Cut spending to rent, food and bills only
Ask Hana's parents about moving in for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. A bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to sort this out if people stop arguing about it. I'd be fairly quiet about it online. At work I'd ask what the plan is for the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still think marketing is a dead end for me. Five years means I could learn a trade properly, maybe something with my hands, before the robots catch up three years later. The time gives me a choice instead of a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start evening classes in electrical work while keeping my job. I'd try to save hard, maybe five or six months. I'd talk to Hana about whether we can afford me on apprentice pay for a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but less trapped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to learn the AI tools in the meantime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, to keep my job longer. Dennis would help. But I'd put most of my energy into the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money. Apprentice pay is maybe half what I earn. Hana's wage helps, but it's tight.

say: I'd say we have **time** if people stop arguing about it.
At work I'd ask what the **plan for the team** is.
think: I privately see marketing as a **dead end** for me.
Five years turns the move to a **trade** into a choice, not a panic.
do: Start **evening classes** in electrical work while keeping my job.
Save toward **five or six months** of costs.
Plan with Hana for a couple of years on **apprentice pay**.
feel: I feel **worried**, but less trapped than with two years.
S3.quote: Five years means I could learn a trade properly, maybe something with my hands, before the robots catch up three years later.
fieldNote: The extra time lets him **retrain** while still earning.
He still expects to **lose** his marketing job, hence alarmed.
**Apprentice pay** at half his salary is his biggest practical worry.

steps.text: Enrol in evening electrical installation classes next term
Build savings to five or six months of costs
Learn basic AI drafting from Dennis to stay longer at the bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That sounds like a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan, and that people should start now. I'd probably say it to my younger cousins more than anyone online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I could cope. With ten years' notice I'd stop pretending this was going away and actually learn the thing I've been avoiding. I'd probably stay in marketing a few years longer and then switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start using the AI tools properly at work. I'd save steadily. In year three or four I'd decide between moving into trade marketing or learning a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a manageable way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would push you to decide in year three or four?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching what happens to people like Dennis. If even the good AI users start losing hours, I'd know it's time to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana and I want to get married in a couple of years. Ten years means I wouldn't have to put that off.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to plan, and people should start now.
I'd tell my **younger cousins** to prepare.
think: I privately think I could **cope** with a decade's warning.
I'd stop avoiding the **AI tools** and learn them properly.
do: Start using **AI tools** properly at work this year.
Decide in year three or four between **trade marketing** and a trade.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but in a manageable way.
S4.quote: With ten years' notice I'd stop pretending this was going away and actually learn the thing I've been avoiding.
fieldNote: Ten years makes him willing to **drop his resistance** to AI.
He'd watch **colleague Dennis** as an early warning sign.
The extra time protects his **wedding plans** with Hana.

steps.text: Use the bakery's AI tool for first drafts of seasonal copy
Put a fixed sum into savings every month
Watch how AI users at the bakery fare before choosing a path

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm not against progress, I'm just slow to trust it, and two years isn't long enough for someone like me to catch up. What would help is paid apprenticeships for adults, so changing trade at 27 or 40 doesn't mean living on half a wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how people like me feel about being slow. I'm not proud of it. It's just how I am, and I'd like help that doesn't make me feel stupid.

headlineQuote: I'm not against progress, I'm just slow to trust it, and two years isn't long enough for someone like me to catch up.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old marketer** at a family-owned regional bakery, writing packaging and radio copy.
He has **never used AI** and only two months saved after a boiler bill.
He sees AI as **business as usual** and blames no one strongly.
He is uneasy in the plateau but **alarmed** when AGI comes within five years.
His fallback is an **electrician's apprenticeship**, using the robot gap as shelter.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most because he's **slow to adapt** and two years is too short.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid adult apprenticeships** so switching trades doesn't halve his wage.
